title: Helium points to a double detonation in supernova 2024kce
freshness: Unreviewed arXiv preprint submitted October 22, 2026; selected within the preferred 15-day window.
excerpt: Astronomers found three helium absorption signatures in SN 2024kce eleven days before its brightest point. Their locations and speeds support a model in which a surface helium explosion triggered the destruction of a white dwarf, though the result remains an unreviewed preprint.
whyItMatters: Type Ia supernovae help measure cosmic distances, yet astronomers still debate how their white dwarfs ignite. A direct helium signature in the fast outer debris gives researchers a new observational test of one leading route: a surface blast that sets off the star's carbon-oxygen core.

whatToExploreNext: How can spectra taken in the first days after a supernova distinguish a helium-shell double detonation from other ways a white dwarf can explode?

body:
## Helium in the fastest debris

Eleven days before supernova 2024kce reached maximum brightness, astronomers split its light into a spectrum stretching from visible colors into the near-infrared. Three absorption features lined up with helium atoms moving outward at about 16,400 kilometres per second. The authors report this as the first detection of helium before maximum light in a thermonuclear supernova.

That timing matters. A supernova spectrum is a chemical barcode, but the layers it reveals change as the expanding debris thins. Very early observations still sample the outermost material, where a white dwarf might retain evidence of how its explosion began.

SN 2024kce was discovered on June 2, 2024, in the remote outskirts of the giant galaxy M49, about 16.5 million parsecs away. It was classified as a peculiar Type Ia supernova three days later. Type Ia events are powered by the thermonuclear disruption of white dwarfs, the compact remains of Sun-like stars. This one was fainter than a typical Type Ia and later developed strong calcium emission, giving it traits of both subluminous Type Ia supernovae and calcium-rich transients.

## Three lines make the case

The strongest near-infrared helium line falls near a carbon line, so one dip in a spectrum would be ambiguous. The team instead used optical and infrared observations taken within an hour of each other. They identified helium absorption at wavelengths of 1.083 and 2.058 micrometres in the infrared and at 7065 angstroms in visible light. All three point to the same outward speed. A fourth helium feature was tentative.

Carbon and magnesium may still contribute to the blended trough near 1.024 micrometres. The important measurement is that the other lines independently show helium. Its speed places it above the photosphere, the effective glowing surface of the expanding debris, which was moving at about 12,500 kilometres per second.

Helium in that high layer is hard to excite with heat alone. It needs energetic electrons produced when gamma rays from radioactive decay scatter through the debris. The observed helium must therefore sit near radioactive material. That pairing is expected after a helium shell on a carbon-oxygen white dwarf detonates and leaves radioactive ash near the surface. The first blast can send a shock inward and ignite the core, producing a second detonation.

## A model, not a direct replay

The researchers compared the spectra with a calculated explosion of a 0.69-solar-mass white dwarf carrying a 0.09-solar-mass helium shell. The model retained 0.051 solar masses of helium between 13,300 and 22,000 kilometres per second, beside radioactive shell ash. It reproduced the early red color, several line velocities, the near-infrared continuum, and the high-speed helium feature.

The fit is strong evidence for a double detonation, but it is still an inference. The calculation misses some spectral details and diverges from later infrared observations as its simplifying assumptions become less reliable. One event also cannot show that every faint Type Ia or calcium-rich supernova shares this origin.

The paper is an unreviewed preprint. If the result holds, it offers a practical lesson for future surveys: catching unusual explosions is only the start. Rapid, simultaneous optical and infrared spectra can preserve the chemical clue that reveals what lit the fuse.
